message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for rasterizing images, now also used for massively parallel compute tasks. |
| **Core count** | Few cores (typically 2–32 in consumer CPUs). | Hundreds to thousands of smaller cores (e.g., 2,000+ in modern GPUs). |
| **Core design** | Complex, high‑performance cores with deep pipelines, large caches, branch prediction, and sophisticated control logic. | Simpler, lightweight cores optimized for throughput; each core does less work but many can run simultaneously. |
| **Instruction set** | Rich, general‑purpose instruction sets (x86, ARM, etc.) with support for complex branching, system calls, and varied data types. | SIMD‑style instruction sets (SIMT in NVIDIA, wavefronts in AMD) that execute the same operation on many data elements at once. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, sophisticated memory controllers, support for virtual memory, page tables, and complex cache coherence protocols. | Smaller per‑core caches, often a unified memory pool shared across all cores; relies on high bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR). |
| **Latency vs throughput** | Optimized for low latency – quick response to individual instructions or small batches. | Optimized for high throughput – can process millions of data points in parallel, tolerating higher latency per operation. |
| **Typical workloads** | Sequential tasks, branching logic, OS kernel operations, database queries, web servers, office applications. | Data‑parallel tasks: rendering pixels/vertices, scientific simulations, machine‑learning inference/training, video encoding/decoding, cryptography. |
| **Programming model** | Single‑threaded or multi‑threaded with complex scheduling; languages like C/C++, Java, Python, etc. | Parallel programming models: CUDA, OpenCL, DirectX, Vulkan, Metal; requires explicit data parallelism. |
| **Energy efficiency** | Higher power per core, but fewer cores overall. | Lower power per core, but many cores can be idle or active depending on workload. |
| **Cost** | Generally cheaper per core, but higher cost per core‑performance for complex tasks. | Cheaper per core, but cost per core‑performance is lower for highly parallel workloads. |

### Why the difference matters

- **Branching**: CPUs handle unpredictable branches efficiently; GPUs suffer performance penalties when threads diverge because they execute the same instruction stream (SIMT).  
- **Cache coherence**: CPUs maintain strict cache coherence across cores; GPUs use simpler coherence or none at all, relying on explicit memory barriers.  
- **Precision**: GPUs historically favored single‑precision floating point for graphics; modern GPUs support double precision but at a higher cost.  
- **Software ecosystem**: CPUs have mature compilers, debuggers, and operating systems; GPUs require specialized SDKs and debugging tools.

In practice, CPUs are the “brain” that orchestrates tasks, while GPUs are the “muscle” that performs large, repetitive calculations in parallel. For many modern applications—especially AI, scientific computing, and real‑time rendering—the best performance comes from offloading suitable portions of the workload to the GPU while keeping control flow and orchestration on the CPU.
